thesis: This episode argues that while YouTube is a strategically valuable asset for Google, its standalone profitability remains uncertain. It also suggests that LinkedIn has created significant market cap for Microsoft, and that Meta should double down on AI and Reality Lab despite short-term investor pain.

claims.claim: YouTube is strategically valuable as a search engine and social media property, but its profitability is unclear.
claims.quote: YouTube was the utility that you uploaded a video to and then you could embed it on your site. Maybe I was weird, but I couldn't imagine starting my day and going to youtube.com and just watching whatever it served me the way that now it's very easy to do that in the app.

claims.claim: YouTube is a strategic asset for Google, but as a standalone business, it may not make money.
claims.quote: YouTube is both the second largest social media property in the world and the second largest search engine in the world. So yeah, A-plus.

claims.claim: YouTube is strategically a very great thing to own, but as a business, it is not clear to me that YouTube makes money.
claims.quote: But as a business, it is not clear to me that YouTube makes money.

claims.claim: YouTube pays out a significant portion of revenue to creators, making it a tough business to run.
claims.quote: Here is what is unique about YouTube versus every other platform is they pay out 55% of revenue on long-form and 45% on shorts directly to creators.

claims.claim: YouTube has generated significant revenue for Google, but its profitability remains uncertain.
claims.quote: When we did the episode, YouTube was doing about $5 billion run rate revenue. It is now $35–$40 billion annual revenue run rate.

claims.claim: YouTube is a strategic acquisition for Google, but its profitability is not clear.
claims.quote: I'll go on record. Youtube was an A-plus acquisition because of the strategic value. Whether it's the second largest search engine second to Google, or the second largest social media property, it is strategically a very great thing to own. Not to mention going into the land of AI training data. But as a business, it is not clear to me that YouTube makes money.

claims.claim: YouTube is a strategic asset for Google, but its profitability is uncertain.
claims.quote: The way that you should look at YouTube is not what is the discounted cash flow of YouTube as an independent business if you look at their profitability today. It's what was the existential risk to Google of not owning YouTube if YouTube became a thing somewhere outside of Google? And that is worth paying a lot for.

claims.claim: LinkedIn has created significant market cap for Microsoft, but it is still an internal asset.
claims.quote: But essentially they created $100 billion of market cap. If you look at what a reasonable multiple would be for LinkedIn if it were an independent company today, it's a big company. It would be over a $100 billion market cap company today. And it's just kind of hanging out inside Microsoft.

claims.claim: Satya Nadella has run Microsoft as a founder, shifting the company's focus towards social networks, collaboration, cloud, and AI.
claims.quote: Satya has run Microsoft as a type of founder. You could call it being a re-founder or even a late stage co-founder. The re-founder doesn't need to have been in the garage from day one. He shifted the company's focus away from a cutthroat culture and competition–only practices towards embracing social networks, collaboration, cloud, and the next wave of AI.

claims.claim: Mark Zuckerberg believes Meta is a good name and that the company should double down on AI and Reality Lab despite short-term investor pain.
claims.quote: I like Meta. It's a good name, you know, finding good short names...this actually was a thing that we talked about for a while because it was pretty clear that Facebook is continuing to grow in importance in the world

claims.claim: Zuckerberg states that the company should not run away from the Facebook brand but rather build an evocative future brand like Meta.
claims.quote: And it was important to me this was also coinciding with a lot of the challenges that we were having, the political brand challenges, different things and a lot of people were proposing that from the perspective of running away from the Facebook brand

claims.claim: Zuckerberg believes that the company should double down on AI infrastructure and Reality Lab, even if investors hate it in the short term.
claims.quote: What we knew was going to be really painful, you know, to go double down on those things and build out the AI infrastructure that we needed to and scale up some of the Reality Lab stuff and I knew that a lot of the investors would hate it, at least in the short term before it's clearly the right thing to do
